text: [PROTOTYPE DEMO DOCUMENT -- NOT AN OFFICIAL TATA HITACHI SERVICE DOCUMENT] HYDRAULIC TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE Excavator Hydraulic System - General Reference 1. PURPOSE This guide provides a general reference for diagnosing slow or weak hydraulic performance on excavators. It is written for the Engineering Memory prototype and reflects common, publicly known hydraulic fault patterns. It does not represent official Tata Hitachi service documentation and should not be used for real maintenance decisions. 2. COMMON SYMPTOM: SLOW OR WEAK OPERATION When boom, arm, or bucket movement becomes slow or loses digging force, the root cause usually falls into one of the following categories: pump wear, filter or line restriction, oil condition, valve sticking, accumulator pressure loss, cylinder internal leakage, or pilot pressure problems. 3. PUMP-RELATED CAUSES Internal pump leakage occurs when pump seals or wear plates degrade, allowing oil to bypass internally instead of building pressure. This is more noticeable under load and often worsens as oil temperature rises, since hot oil is thinner and bypasses more easily. Symptom pattern: gradual power loss across all functions, worse when hot. 4. COOLING-RELATED CAUSES A restricted oil cooler reduces the system's ability to shed heat. As oil temperature climbs, viscosity drops and internal leakage increases across every component, which is why cooler restriction often looks identical to pump wear at first glance. Check cooler fins for debris and confirm the cooling fan is operating before assuming a pump fault. 5. FILTER AND LINE RESTRICTION A clogged return filter or suction strainer restricts oil flow, causing jerky or inconsistent movement rather than a smooth power loss. This symptom pattern (inconsistent, not gradual) helps distinguish filter issues from pump wear. Check filter bypass indicators first, since this is the fastest and cheapest check to rule out. 6. Check filter bypass indicators first, since this is the fastest and cheapest check to rule out. 6. VALVE PROBLEMS A sticking spool valve, often caused by varnish buildup in older or contaminated oil, causes uneven response between functions. One function may work normally while another lags. This asymmetry across functions is the key distinguishing sign versus a system-wide pump or cooler issue. 7. ACCUMULATOR PRESSURE LOSS Low accumulator pre-charge pressure causes a delayed or jerky start when a function is first engaged, but normal operation once running. This "jerky start, smooth after" pattern is distinct from a continuous slowness pattern. 8. OIL CONTAMINATION Particulate or water contamination in the hydraulic oil affects every function simultaneously and often correlates with unusual noise. An oil sample analysis is the most reliable way to confirm this versus assuming a mechanical fault. 9. CYLINDER INTERNAL LEAKAGE A cylinder with a worn piston seal will drift down under load or lose force in one specific function while others remain normal. This is similar in presentation to a valve problem but is isolated to a single actuator rather than a control path. 10. PILOT PRESSURE PROBLEMS Low pilot pressure causes levers to feel "light" or unresponsive across multiple functions, distinct from a hydraulic power loss because the main pump and valves may test normally. Check the pilot pressure reducing valve and pilot filter first. 11. RECOMMENDED DIAGNOSTIC ORDER Check the cheapest and fastest items first: filter bypass indicator, oil level and visible contamination, cooler fin cleanliness. Then check pressure readings (main and pilot). Only after ruling out these should pump or cylinder teardown be considered, since these are the most costly to

PURPOSE This SOP describes the standard steps for inspecting and replacing hydraulic filters (return line filter and suction strainer) on excavators, written for the Engineering Memory prototype as demo reference data. 2. WHEN TO INSPECT Inspect filters when the bypass indicator is triggered, when jerky or inconsistent hydraulic response is reported, after any major hydraulic component repair, or at the standard scheduled service interval. 3. SAFETY PREPARATION Shut down the engine and relieve system pressure before opening any filter housing. Allow hot oil to cool to a safe handling temperature. Have a drain pan ready to catch residual oil. 4. RETURN LINE FILTER REPLACEMENT Step 1: Locate the return line filter housing near the hydraulic tank. Step 2: Clean the exterior of the housing before opening to prevent debris entry. Step 3: Remove the housing cap and extract the filter element. Step 4: Inspect the old element for metal particles, which may indicate pump or component wear upstream. Step 5: Install a new filter element of the correct part specification. Step 6: Reassemble the housing and torque to specification. Step 7: Start the engine and check for leaks at the housing. 5. SUCTION STRAINER CLEANING Step 1: Drain the hydraulic tank to below the strainer level. Step 2: Remove the strainer access panel. Step 3: Extract and clean the strainer mesh using an approved solvent. Step 4: Inspect the mesh for tears or damage; replace if compromised. Step 5: Reinstall the strainer and access panel. RELATED SYMPTOMS Filter blockage typically presents as inconsistent or jerky movement across functions rather than a gradual, uniform power loss. If symptoms persist after filter replacement, investigate pump or valve causes next.

[PROTOTYPE DEMO DOCUMENT -- NOT AN OFFICIAL TATA HITACHI SERVICE DOCUMENT] COOLING SYSTEM - STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE Excavator Hydraulic Oil Cooler - Inspection and Service 1. PURPOSE This SOP describes standard steps for inspecting and servicing the hydraulic oil cooler on excavators, written for the Engineering Memory prototype as demo reference data. 2. WHEN TO INSPECT Inspect the cooler when oil temperature readings trend higher than normal, when hydraulic performance degrades after extended operating periods (a pattern often described as "fine in the morning, slow by afternoon"), or at the standard scheduled service interval. 3. SAFETY PREPARATION Shut down the engine and allow the cooler and surrounding components to cool before inspection. Wear eye protection when using compressed air or a pressure washer near the cooler fins. 4. VISUAL INSPECTION Step 1: Locate the oil cooler, typically mounted near the radiator. Step 2: Visually inspect the fins for dirt, mud, or debris buildup. Step 3: Check for bent or damaged fins that would restrict airflow. Step 4: Inspect the cooling fan belt for wear, cracking, or looseness. 5. CLEANING PROCEDURE Step 1: Use low-pressure compressed air or a pressure washer, directed opposite to normal airflow, to clear debris from the fins. Step 2: Avoid bending fins during cleaning; work in small sections. Step 3: Inspect fan belt tension and adjust or replace if loose or worn. Step 4: Confirm the cooling fan spins freely with no obstruction. 6. POST-SERVICE CHECKS After cleaning, run the machine under normal working load for at least 30 minutes and monitor oil temperature. Confirm temperature stabilizes within the normal operating range rather than continuing to climb. 7.
